passages.text: Functional Validation of <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> Variants Identified in a Neural Tube Defect Cohort Demonstrates Their Contribution to Neural Tube Defects

Neural tube defects (NTDs) are severe malformations of the central nervous system that affect 1-2 individuals per 2,000 births. <sentence_start/>Their etiology is complex and involves both genetic and environmental factors. <sentence_start/>Our recent discovery that simultaneous removal of Cldn3, -4, and -8 from tight junctions results in cranial and spinal NTDs in both chick and mouse embryos suggests that claudins play a conserved role in neural tube closure in vertebrates. <sentence_start/>To determine if claudins were associated with NTDs in humans, we used a Fluidigm next generation sequencing approach to identify genetic variants in <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> loci in 152 patients with spinal NTDs. <sentence_start/>We identified eleven rare and four novel missense mutations in ten <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> genes. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">In vivo</italic> validation of variant pathogenicity using a chick embryo model system revealed that overexpression of four variants caused a significant increase in NTDs: <italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic> A128T, <italic toggle="yes">CLDN8</italic> P216L, <italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic> I22T, and E209G. Our data implicate rare missense variants in <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> genes as risk factors for spinal NTDs and suggest a new family of proteins involved in the pathogenesis of these malformations.
Introduction

Neural tube defects (NTDs) [MIM: 182940] are a group of congenital central nervous system malformations that affect the brain and spinal cord, caused by failure of neural tube closure during embryogenesis. <sentence_start/>They have a complex etiology involving both genetic and environmental factors. <sentence_start/>The two most common forms are the cranial defect, anencephaly, and the spinal defect, myelomeningocele (spina bifida). <sentence_start/>A third rare form of open NTDs, craniorachischisis, occurs when the neural tube fails to close along the entire length of the body axis. <sentence_start/>NTDs are the second most common birth defect with a varying incidence, affecting 1-2 per 2,000 pregnancies in North America post-folic acid fortification, and as high as 20 per 1,000 births in certain regions of China (<citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0895-3988(09)60065-9" pmid="19950530" count="1">Chen et al., 2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Approximately 300,000 newborns affected by these defects are born annually (<citation rid="B96" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0151586" pmid="27064786" pmcid="PMC4827875" count="1">Zaganjor et al., 2016</citation>). <sentence_start/>Thus, there is an urgent need to better understand the underlying pathogenic mechanisms of NTDs, particularly those not prevented by folic acid fortification.

Neural tube closure, which occurs during the fourth week of human gestation, is divided into four distinct phases (<citation rid="B90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cells8101198" pmid="31590237" pmcid="PMC6829399" count="1">Wang et al., 2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>First, a subset of medial ectodermal cells is induced to differentiate into neural progenitors, which form the neural plate. <sentence_start/>Next, the neural plate undergoes convergent extension, which leads to its mediolateral narrowing and anterior-posterior extension. <sentence_start/>This is followed by apical constriction of midline cells to form the median hinge point, which allows the neural plate to bend at the midline and the lateral edges of the neural plate to elevate and become the neural folds. <sentence_start/>Finally, the lateral edges of the neural folds meet at the dorsal midline where they fuse to generate a closed neural tube and a contiguous overlying layer of surface ectoderm.

A defect in any of these phases of neural tube closure will result in a NTD. <sentence_start/>Defects in convergent extension, which is regulated by the non-canonical Wnt/planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway, result in NTDs due to the fact that the lateral edges of the neural folds never come in close enough proximity to fuse. <sentence_start/>Many animal models with mutations in PCP components develop NTDs due to aberrant convergent extension movements (<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0925-4773(98)00029-x" pmid="9545534" count="1">Greene et al., 1998</citation>; <citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1006/dbio.2002.0673" pmid="12074560" count="1">Goto and Keller, 2002</citation>; <citation rid="B87" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/dev.00123" pmid="12421719" count="1">Wallingford and Harland, 2002</citation>; <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0960-9822(03)00374-9" pmid="12842012" count="1">Curtin et al., 2003</citation>; <citation rid="B88" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/dev.02347" pmid="16571627" pmcid="PMC4158842" count="1">Wang J. et al., 2006</citation>; <citation rid="B89" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/jneurosci.4698-05.2005" pmid="16495441" pmcid="PMC6674805" count="1">Wang Y. et al., 2006</citation>; <citation rid="B94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/dev.000380" pmid="17229766" pmcid="PMC1839770" count="1">Ybot-Gonzalez et al., 2007</citation>; <citation rid="B58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-213X-10-87" pmid="20704721" pmcid="PMC2930600" count="1">Paudyal et al., 2010</citation>) and rare and novel missense mutations in PCP genes are risk factors for NTDs in humans (<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19319979" doi="10.1002/humu.21026" pmcid="PMC2885434" count="1">Kibar et al., 2009</citation>, <citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1399-0004.2010.01515.x" pmid="20738329" pmcid="PMC3000889" count="1">2011</citation>; <citation rid="B43" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20558380" doi="10.1056/NEJMc0910820" count="1">Lei et al., 2010</citation>, <citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mgg3.584" pmid="30689296" pmcid="PMC6465732" count="1">2019</citation>; <citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.21589" pmid="21901791" pmcid="PMC3217084" count="1">Bosoi et al., 2011</citation>; <citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/bdra.23002" pmid="22371354" count="1">Allache et al., 2012</citation>; <citation rid="B17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.21643" pmid="22045688" pmcid="PMC3482927" count="1">De Marco et al., 2012</citation>, <citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12031-012-9871-9" pmid="22892949" pmcid="PMC3566388" count="1">2013</citation>; <citation rid="B62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.21662" pmid="22095531" pmcid="PMC4772123" count="1">Robinson et al., 2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>The PCP pathway is one of the few candidate pathways identified in animal models whose human homologs have been shown to contribute to risk of human NTDs. <sentence_start/>Formation of the hinge points requires RhoA/ROCK-mediated actin-myosin contraction of the apical surface of neural plate cells (<citation rid="B37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1091/mbc.e07-12-1286" pmid="18337466" pmcid="PMC2366863" count="1">Kinoshita et al., 2008</citation>; <citation rid="B65" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ydbio.2008.12.009" pmid="19121300" pmcid="PMC2820227" count="1">Rolo et al., 2009</citation>; <citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/jcs.164574" pmid="26040287" pmcid="PMC4510849" count="1">Escuin et al., 2015</citation>).

We recently discovered that claudins act upstream of the PCP and RhoA/ROCK signaling pathways to regulate cell shape changes and tissue movements during neural tube morphogenesis (<citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ydbio.2017.05.013" pmid="28545845" pmcid="PMC5523803" count="1">Baumholtz et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>Indeed, simultaneous removal of Cldn3, -4, and -8 from tight junctions causes open NTDs in both chick and mouse embryos (<citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ydbio.2017.05.013" pmid="28545845" pmcid="PMC5523803" count="1">Baumholtz et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>Claudins comprise a family of integral tight junction proteins with ∼24 unique members in vertebrates. <sentence_start/>They have four transmembrane domains, two extracellular loops, and cytoplasmic N- and C-termini. <sentence_start/>The first extracellular loop contains charged amino acids that determine the ion and size selectivity of the tight junction paracellular barrier (<citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.136.6.1239" pmid="9087440" pmcid="PMC2132509" count="1">Katahira et al., 1997</citation>; <citation rid="B29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.m109005200" pmid="11689568" count="1">Hamazaki et al., 2002</citation>; <citation rid="B75" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.modgep.2004.10.009" pmid="15749086" count="1">Simard et al., 2005</citation>; <citation rid="B61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1462-5822.2007.00994.x" pmid="17587331" count="1">Robertson et al., 2007</citation>; <citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ydbio.2017.05.013" pmid="28545845" pmcid="PMC5523803" count="1">Baumholtz et al., 2017</citation>; <citation rid="B53" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-019-08760-7" pmid="30778075" pmcid="PMC6379431" count="1">Nakamura et al., 2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>The second extracellular loop participates in <italic toggle="yes">trans</italic>-interactions with claudin molecules in apposing cells, and in <italic toggle="yes">cis</italic>-interactions with other claudins in the same cell (<citation rid="B60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fj.07-8319com" pmid="17761522" count="1">Piontek et al., 2008</citation>; <citation rid="B81" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.1248571" pmid="24744376" count="1">Suzuki et al., 2014</citation>). <sentence_start/>The transmembrane domains also participate in <italic toggle="yes">cis</italic>-oligomerization (<citation rid="B66" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.m113.531012" pmid="24478310" pmcid="PMC3953276" count="1">Rossa et al., 2014</citation>). <sentence_start/>Together, these interactions constitute the backbone of tight junction strands and prevent the mixing of apical and basolateral proteins (<citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.semcdb.2015.04.010" pmid="25957516" count="1">Krause et al., 2015</citation>). <sentence_start/>The claudin cytoplasmic C-terminal tail has a conserved PDZ-binding domain that interacts with adaptor proteins at the tight junction cytoplasmic plaque, thereby linking the tight junction to the actin cytoskeleton and intracellular signaling events (<citation rid="B86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.m113.466193" pmid="23553632" pmcid="PMC3650414" count="1">Van Itallie et al., 2013</citation>; <citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0117074" pmid="25789658" pmcid="PMC4366163" count="1">Fredriksson et al., 2015</citation>; <citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ydbio.2017.05.013" pmid="28545845" pmcid="PMC5523803" count="1">Baumholtz et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>The C-terminal domain also contains numerous phosphorylation sites that can influence protein interactions at the tight junction cytoplasmic plaque (<citation rid="B83" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.m503786200" pmid="16236711" count="1">Tanaka et al., 2005</citation>; <citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/jcs.02901" pmid="16608877" count="1">Ikari et al., 2006</citation>).

Given the importance of claudins in neural tube closure in chick and mouse, we tested our hypothesis that mutations in <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> genes are risk factors for human NTDs by screening a cohort of 152 open spinal NTD patients for rare and novel non-synonymous <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> variants. <sentence_start/>We identified 11 rare and four novel missense variants in 10 <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> genes. <sentence_start/>We then tested the functional consequences of the <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> variants by transfection of HEK293 or MDCK II cells to determine if the variant protein localized to the tight junction and then by overexpressing the variants in chick embryos to determine if the variants caused defects in neural tube closure. <sentence_start/>Our data suggest that rare missense mutations in <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> genes are risk factors for human NTDs.
Subjects and Methods
Neural Tube Defect Cohort

The studies involving human participants were reviewed and approved by IRCCS Istituto Giannina Gaslini (Protocol number: IGG-VACA, 18 September 2011) and the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre (Protocol number: 14-444-PED). <sentence_start/>Written informed consent to participate in this study was provided by the participants and/or their legal guardian/next of kin. <sentence_start/>The patient cohort consisted of 152 unrelated individuals with myelomeningocele, who were recruited at the Spina Bifida Center of the Gaslini Hospital in Genova, Italy, between the period of 2006-2017. <sentence_start/>The age of patients ranged from 3 to 20 years, with the mean age being 9.6 years. <sentence_start/>The female/male ratio was 1.2. <sentence_start/>All participants were Italians with antecedents from all parts of the country. <sentence_start/>The majority of these individuals were of European ancestry, although some individuals were of Hispanic or African ancestry. <sentence_start/>Upon entering the study, individuals were re-evaluated by a clinical geneticist and diagnosis was made on the basis of MRI, X-ray images and clinical records, according to previously described criteria (<citation rid="B67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ejrad.2003.10.015" pmid="15081131" count="1">Rossi et al., 2004</citation>). <sentence_start/>The study group includes individuals who were previously analyzed for mutation of PCP genes (<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19319979" doi="10.1002/humu.21026" pmcid="PMC2885434" count="1">Kibar et al., 2009</citation>, <citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1399-0004.2010.01515.x" pmid="20738329" pmcid="PMC3000889" count="1">2011</citation>; <citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.21589" pmid="21901791" pmcid="PMC3217084" count="1">Bosoi et al., 2011</citation>; <citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/bdra.23002" pmid="22371354" count="1">Allache et al., 2012</citation>; <citation rid="B17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.21643" pmid="22045688" pmcid="PMC3482927" count="1">De Marco et al., 2012</citation>, <citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12031-012-9871-9" pmid="22892949" pmcid="PMC3566388" count="1">2013</citation>; <citation rid="B62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.21662" pmid="22095531" pmcid="PMC4772123" count="1">Robinson et al., 2012</citation>).
Next-Generation DNA Sequencing

Genomic DNA was isolated from blood samples using the QIAamp DNA blood kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Qiagen, Milan, Italy). <sentence_start/>The genomic sequence of <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic>s was determined using the UCSC Genome Browser assembly ID hg19 (<italic toggle="yes">CLDN1</italic>: RefSeq [MIM: 607626]; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN2</italic>: RefSeq , <italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic>: RefSeq ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN4</italic>: RefSeq ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN5</italic>: GenBank ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN6</italic>: GenBank <italic toggle="yes">N</italic>C_000016.9; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN7</italic>: GenBank <italic toggle="yes">N</italic>C_000017.10; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN8</italic>: RefSeq ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN9</italic>: ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN10</italic>: RefSeq [MIM: 617671]; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN11</italic>: GenBank ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN12</italic>: GenBank ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN14</italic>: GenBank [MIM: 614035]; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN15</italic>: GenBank ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN16</italic>: RefSeq [MIM: 248250]; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN17</italic>: GenBank ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN18</italic>: GenBank ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic>: RefSeq [MIM: 248190]; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN20</italic>: RefSeq ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN21</italic>: RefSeq ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN22</italic>: RefSeq ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN23</italic>: GenBank ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN24</italic>: RefSeq ; <italic toggle="yes">CLDN25</italic>: GenBank ). <sentence_start/>DNA was then processed by microfluidic polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using a custom Fluidigm Access Array, followed by next-generation sequencing on an Illumina MiSeq platform at the McGill University and Genome Quebec Innovation Center (Montreal, QC, Canada). <sentence_start/>Briefly, 92 custom pairs of primers were designed to amplify ∼300 bp fragments of the coding exons of the 24 human claudin genes (Supplementary Table S1). <sentence_start/>Primer sets were validated using a standard PCR protocol to ensure that they amplified a single fragment of the expected size, and selected amplicons were validated by Sanger sequencing. <sentence_start/>The amplicons from the array were pooled and the resulting pools were multiplexed and sequenced using the Illumina MiSeq. <sentence_start/>Reads were processed and aligned to the human genome (UCSC hg19, NCBI build 37) by Genome Quebec. <sentence_start/>Aligned and processed BAM files were used to manually identify variants using the Integrative Genomics Viewer version 2.3 (<citation rid="B64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nbt.1754" pmid="21221095" pmcid="PMC3346182" count="1">Robinson et al., 2011</citation>, <citation rid="B63" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.Can-17-0337" pmid="29092934" pmcid="PMC5678989" count="1">2017</citation>; <citation rid="B84" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bib/bbs017" pmid="22517427" pmcid="PMC3603213" count="1">Thorvaldsdottir et al., 2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>Variants with alternative allele frequencies of 30% or greater were selected for further analysis.
Sanger Sequencing of CLDN3

The single <italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic> coding exon was amplified by PCR using a single primer pair (Supplementary Table S2) and subjected to Sanger sequencing at the McGill University and Genome Quebec Innovation Centre (Montreal, QC, Canada). <sentence_start/>Samples were sequenced in both directions using specific forward and reverse primers. <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic> variants were confirmed by repeating the PCR and re-sequencing from a single direction.
Bioinformatics

Variants were annotated according to the HGVS nomenclature<sup>1</sup>. <sentence_start/>The Exome Variant Server (EVS<sup>2</sup> (<citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Exome Variant Server, 2020</citation>) and Genome Aggregation Database v2.1.1 (gnomAD<sup>3</sup> (<citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/531210" pmcid="PMC7334197" pmid="32461654" count="1">Karczewski et al., 2020</citation>) public databases were queried for the presence and incidence of the variants identified in <italic toggle="yes">CLDN1-25</italic>. <sentence_start/>Rare variants were defined as having a minor allele frequency (MAF) < 1% in these databases and novel variants were defined as those not present in these databases. <sentence_start/>The potential pathogenic effect of the identified mutations on protein function was predicted using three software programs: Polymorphism Phenotyping v2 (PolyPhen-2<sup>4</sup>; <citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nmeth0410-248" pmid="20354512" pmcid="PMC2855889" count="1">Adzhubei et al., 2010</citation>), Sorting Intolerant from Tolerant (SIFT<sup>5</sup>) (<citation rid="B55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gkg509" pmid="12824425" pmcid="PMC168916" count="1">Ng and Henikoff, 2003</citation>) and MutationTaster<sup>6</sup> (<citation rid="B73" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nmeth0810-575" pmid="20676075" count="1">Schwarz et al., 2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Multiple alignments of the CLDN proteins were done using the Clustal Omega program<sup>7</sup>. <sentence_start/>Localization of the variants in protein domains was assessed by Uniprot<sup>8</sup>. <sentence_start/>Predicted phosphorylation sites in CLDN proteins were identified using NetPhos 3.1<sup>9</sup> (<citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1006/jmbi.1999.3310" pmid="10600390" count="1">Blom et al., 1999</citation>).
DNA Resequencing of <italic toggle="yes">CLDNs</italic>

Rare and novel missense variants were validated by Sanger sequencing. <sentence_start/>Primers flanking the coding exons of <italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic> (RefSeq ), <italic toggle="yes">CLDN4</italic> (RefSeq ), <italic toggle="yes">CLDN6</italic> (RefSeq ), <italic toggle="yes">CLDN8</italic> (RefSeq ), <italic toggle="yes">CLDN9</italic> (RefSeq ), <italic toggle="yes">CLDN14</italic> (RefSeq ), <italic toggle="yes">CLDN16</italic> (RefSeq ), <italic toggle="yes">CLDN18</italic> (RefSeq ), <italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic> (RefSeq ), <italic toggle="yes">CLDN23</italic> (RefSeq ), <italic toggle="yes">CLDN24</italic> (RefSeq ) were used to amplify the coding region by polymerase chain reaction (Supplementary Table S2). <sentence_start/>Amplicons were subjected to Sanger sequencing at the McGill University and Genome Quebec Innovation Centre (Montreal, QC, Canada).
Generation of Claudin Wild-Type and Mutant Constructs

The full-length human wild-type and variant sequences for claudins encoded by a single exon (<italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">4</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">6</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">24</italic>) were amplified from genomic DNA of NTD patients by PCR and cloned into the pSCA vector using the Stratagene PCR cloning kit (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, United States). <sentence_start/>pMXs-Puro-CLDN18 was a gift from Axel Hillmer (Addgene plasmid #69466) (<citation rid="B93" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26146084" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2015.06.020" count="1">Yao et al., 2015</citation>) and used as a template to clone full-length CLDN18 into pSCA. <italic toggle="yes">CLDN16</italic> p.N223S, <italic toggle="yes">CLDN18</italic> p.V88I and <italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic> p.I22T were introduced in the pSCA-claudin constructs by site-directed mutagenesis using the Stratagene QuikChange II Site-Directed Mutagenesis kit according to manufacturer’s directions (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, United States). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic> p.E209G was created by PCR using a reverse primer containing the mutation and pSCA-HCLDN19 as a template. <sentence_start/>Sequence identity of cDNA clones was confirmed by sequencing at the McGill University and Genome Quebec Innovation Centre (Montreal, QC, Canada). <sentence_start/>Wild-type and variant constructs were then cloned into the pCanHA3 and pMES-IRES-GFP expression plasmids. <sentence_start/>Primer sequences used for mutagenesis reactions are shown in Supplementary Table S3.
Immunolocalization of Ectopically Expressed Claudins

HEK293 and MDCK II cells were grown in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and antibiotics. <sentence_start/>HEK293 cells were plated on coverslips in a 24-well plate and reached 70-90% confluence the day of the transfection experiments. <sentence_start/>pMES or pCanHA3 expression vectors encoding wild-type or variant claudins were transiently transfected into HEK293 cells using Lipofectamine LTX (Invitrogen) in a 1:1 DNA-reagent ratio using 500 ng of plasmid DNA per well. <sentence_start/>MDCK II cells were transfected in suspension using Polyjet (FroggaBio) in a 4:1 DNA-reagent ratio using 500 ng plasmid per well and plated on coverslips in a 24-well plate at 70% confluency. <sentence_start/>HEK293 and MDCK II cells were cultured for 24 h after transfection. <sentence_start/>After rinsing with PBS, cells were fixed with 10% trichloroacetic acid or 4% PFA for 10 min at 4°C, blocked with 10% normal goat serum in 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS and then incubated with primary antibody for 1 h at room temperature. <sentence_start/>Primary antibodies used were Cldn3 and 16 (Abcam, Cambridge, United Kingdom, 1:100), Cldn8 (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, United States, 1:100), ZO-1 (Invitrogen, 1:100, Carlsbad, CA, United States), and HA (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, United States, 1:100). <sentence_start/>Antibodies were detected with Alexa Fluor<sup>®</sup> 488 conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG and Alexa Fluor<sup>®</sup> 594 conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (Molecular Probes). <sentence_start/>Slides were coverslipped with SlowFade Gold Antifade kit (Molecular Probes), which contained DAPI to enable visualization of the nuclei, and imaged using a laser scanning confocal microscope (LSM780, Leica, Germany).
Overexpression Assay in the Chick Embryo

CLDN-IRES-GFP pMES expression vectors (5 μg/μl) were injected into the space between the vitelline membrane and the epiblast of HH4 embryos cultured <italic toggle="yes">ex ovo</italic> on agar-albumen plates using a Narishige IM 300 microinjector, and then electroporated using a Protech CUY21SC square electroporator (five 3 V/50 ms pulses at 500 ms intervals). <sentence_start/>Manipulated embryos were cultured at 39.5°C until HH11-13 and then scored for defects in neural tube closure and convergent extension. <sentence_start/>Brightfield and GFP images of electroporated embryos were taken using a Leica M205FA dissecting microscope and Leica DFC450C camera with Leica Application Suite X software. <sentence_start/>Only embryos with GFP expression in neural and non-neural ectoderm cells were included for phenotype evaluation.
Assessment of Axial Length

Dorsal images of HH12 embryos (somite stage 15-17) were photographed using a Leica M125 dissecting microscope and imported into ImageJ software. <sentence_start/>Axial length was measured from the tip of the forebrain to the tip of the tail bud.
Whole Mount <italic toggle="yes">in situ</italic> Hybridization

Whole-mount <italic toggle="yes">in situ</italic> hybridization was performed as previously described (<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/978-1-61779-185-7_14" pmid="21717358" count="1">Collins and Ryan, 2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Embryos were photographed using a Leica M125 dissecting microscope with Infinity Capture software v5.0.2 (Lumenera Corp.). <sentence_start/>Paraffin-embedded embryos were sectioned and photographed using a Zeiss Axiophot compound microscope and AxioCamMRc camera with Axiovision v4.7.1.0 software.
Histology

Embryos were fixed overnight in 4% paraformaldehyde, dehydrated in a graded ethanol series and embedded in paraffin wax. <sentence_start/>Seven-micron sections were stained using Mayer’s hematoxylin solution and Eosin Y (both Sigma). <sentence_start/>Images were captured on a Leica DM6000B upright microscope equipped with a DFC450C camera.
Statistical Analyses

To examine the association of <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> mutations in the etiology of human NTDs, we sequenced the coding region of the 24 human <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> genes in 152 patients with open spinal NTDs (myelomeningocele) by targeted next generation sequencing. <sentence_start/>Recent publications of large population sequencing data provide an opportunity to characterize with accuracy and precision the frequency distributions of rare disease-causing alleles. <sentence_start/>Since we did not have an adequate control group for size and for ethnicity, we decided to use the Exome Variant Server (EVS) (<citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Exome Variant Server, 2020</citation>) that catalogs whole exome sequencing data of 6503 unrelated European and African Americans, and the gnomAD database (<citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/531210" pmcid="PMC7334197" pmid="32461654" count="1">Karczewski et al., 2020</citation>) that provides variants from 125,748 exomes and 15,708 genomes of unrelated individuals for making inferences on the overall role of <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> variants. <sentence_start/>Importantly, neither database contains individuals with severe congenital anomalies. <sentence_start/>The EVS database contains healthy controls and extremes of specific adult onset traits and/or diseases, including blood pressure, early onset myocardial infarction and stroke, and lung disease. <sentence_start/>In the gnomAD database, individuals affected by severe pediatric disease, and their first-degree relatives, were removed. <sentence_start/>Thus, neither database contains individuals with myelomeningocele open NTDs, supporting their use as appropriate control populations for our study cohort. <sentence_start/>The individuals in these databases are adults, and therefore, deleterious variants for any gene that have the potential to contribute to conditions associated with early mortality may be underrepresented. <sentence_start/>To date, gnomAD is the largest and most comprehensive source of genetic information of individuals of different ethnic backgrounds and similar to our cohort, the largest ethnicity represented is non-Finnish Europeans. <sentence_start/>However, neither database provides precise ancestry information. <sentence_start/>Another potential limitation to the database is that the sequencing data are derived from different exome capture approaches and sequencing platforms, which leads to variation in coverage between individuals and across sites. <sentence_start/>While this may impact the exact allele frequency, the large number of individuals that have been analyzed allows us to distinguish between common, rare and novel variants. <sentence_start/>With respect to our own data, we only considered variants where the alternate allele was present in at least 30% of the sequencing reads.

Claudins are able to localize to cell-cell contacts and induce the formation of tight junction strands when transfected in tight junction-free HEK293 cells (<citation rid="B48" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1042/bj20150148" pmid="25849148" count="1">Milatz et al., 2015</citation>; <citation rid="B59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/nyas.13341" pmid="28415153" count="1">Piontek et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>To determine if the <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> variants identified in the NTD patients affected the ability of the CLDN protein to localize to the cell membrane, we transiently transfected HEK293 cells with expression vectors containing the wild-type or variant <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> cDNA. <sentence_start/>The ability of the claudin to co-localize with ZO-1, a classic component of the tight junction cytoplasmic plaque (<citation rid="B80" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.103.3.755" pmid="3528172" pmcid="PMC2114282" count="1">Stevenson et al., 1986</citation>, <citation rid="B79" ref-type="bibr" pmid="2679124" doi="10.1152/ajpcell.1989.257.4.C621" count="1">1989</citation>), was assessed. <sentence_start/>Wild-type and variant CLDN3, CLDN8, CLDN16, and CLDN19 proteins were able to co-localize with ZO-1 at points of cell-cell contact between neighboring transfected HEK 293 claudin-expressing cells (Figure 3), suggesting that these amino acid substitutions do not impact the ability of variant CLDN to integrate into a tight junction strand. <sentence_start/>Although the CLDN18 V88I protein was localized to cell-cell contacts, it appeared to be less tightly associated with the membrane than wild-type CLDN18.

Discussion

Previously we showed that depletion of Cldn3, -4, and -8 from tight junctions in the neural (Cldn4 and -8) and non-neural ectoderm (Cldn3 and -4) results in NTDs in chick and mouse embryos (<citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ydbio.2017.05.013" pmid="28545845" pmcid="PMC5523803" count="1">Baumholtz et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>Morphological analysis of chick embryos revealed that these claudins play critical roles in regulating convergent extension and apical constriction, two morphogenetic events that drive neural tube closure (<citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ydbio.2017.05.013" pmid="28545845" pmcid="PMC5523803" count="1">Baumholtz et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, the possible contribution of rare and novel mutations in <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> genes to human NTDs has not yet been studied. <sentence_start/>Using a targeted high-throughput sequencing strategy for <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> genes, we identified 17 common, 11 rare and four novel variants in a cohort of 152 NTD patients with the open spinal NTD myelomeningocele. <sentence_start/>Eight of the rare variants (<italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic> p.P134L, <italic toggle="yes">CLDN8</italic> p.P216L, <italic toggle="yes">CLDN9</italic> p.S3L, <italic toggle="yes">CLDN16</italic> p.N223S, <italic toggle="yes">CLDN18</italic> p.V88I, <italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic> p.I22T and p.E209G, and <italic toggle="yes">CLDN24</italic> p.E161K) and two of the novel <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> variants (<italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic> p.A128T and <italic toggle="yes">CLDN24</italic> p.G94R) were predicted to be pathogenic by at least one prediction program. <sentence_start/>Overexpression assays in a chick embryo model demonstrated that <italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic> A128T, <italic toggle="yes">CLDN8</italic> P216L, and <italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic> I22T and E209G generated a significant increase in open NTDs compared to overexpression of the ‘empty’ vector or the wild-type <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic>. <sentence_start/>All of these variants appear to localize normally to tight junctions at cell-cell contacts, which suggests that they may contribute to NTDs by interfering with protein-protein interactions at the tight junction. <sentence_start/>Our data suggest that variants in CLDN proteins may underlie a subset of human NTDs.

Pathogenic <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> variants could affect neural tube closure by three possible mechanisms. <sentence_start/>First, they may function as null alleles due to effects on protein stability, function or tight junction localization and cause NTDs due to insufficient levels of the claudin protein at the tight junction. <sentence_start/>Second, the variant may lead to the production of a dominant negative protein that could compete with wild-type protein for incorporation into tight junction strands, but once there it would the impede the function of wild-type claudins. <sentence_start/>Finally, the variant may predispose an individual to having an NTD but be insufficient to independently cause an NTD. <sentence_start/>In these cases, we would predict that a ‘second hit’ such as a variant in another claudin family member or a component of an intersecting pathway would be required to induce NTDs.

None of the <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> variants that we identified in this myelomeningocele cohort were truncating alleles nor predicted to generate a null allele. <sentence_start/>Moreover, we did not expect a claudin null allele to cause an NTD given that none of the <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> null mice have NTDs (<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0092-8674(00)81553-6" pmid="10612400" count="1">Gow et al., 1999</citation>; Our overexpression functional assay in chick embryos is most effective at identifying variants that have the potential to act as ‘dominant negatives’ or ‘competitive inhibitors’ since we are expressing them in the context of a full complement of wild-type claudins. <sentence_start/>We noted that overexpression of wild-type <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic>s did not cause NTDs suggesting that higher levels of a wild-type claudin protein are not pathogenic. <sentence_start/>We tested the functional pathogenicity of nine variants that were predicted to be pathogenic by one or more analysis software programs. <sentence_start/>Four of these variants caused open NTDs when overexpressed in chick embryos, while overexpression of the corresponding wild-type <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> did not. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, the distinct phenotypes observed when pathogenic variants were overexpressed in chick embryos correlate with the position of the variant in the claudin protein and suggest that claudins function in multiple phases of neural tube closure. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic> I22T and <italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic> A128T, which are in the first and third transmembrane domains, respectively, caused a significant increase in NTDs in chick embryos due to defects in the fusion of the neural folds to form a closed neural tube. <sentence_start/>Both variants change the amino acid in the transmembrane domain to a threonine, which has the potential to disrupt heteromeric <italic toggle="yes">cis-</italic>interactions between claudins and the morphology of tight junction strands (<citation rid="B66" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.m113.531012" pmid="24478310" pmcid="PMC3953276" count="1">Rossa et al., 2014</citation>). <sentence_start/>In addition, <italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic> p.I22T, but not <italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic> p.A128T, introduces a putative phosphorylation site that could induce a further conformational change. <sentence_start/>These alterations to tight junction morphology could affect tight junction barrier properties.

The mechanism by which <italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic> could regulate neural fold fusion remains unknown, but may relate to their function in regulating the tight junction barrier. <sentence_start/>In addition, <italic toggle="yes">Cldn3</italic> expression is limited to the non-neural ectoderm (<citation rid="B76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.mod.2005.12.004" pmid="16500087" count="1">Simard et al., 2006</citation>; <citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ydbio.2017.05.013" pmid="28545845" pmcid="PMC5523803" count="1">Baumholtz et al., 2017</citation>), which functions primarily in neural fold fusion. <sentence_start/>The initial contact between apposing neural folds is mediated by extracellular matrix proteins secreted from the neural and non-neural ectoderm in the chick embryo. <sentence_start/>It was shown that Cldn3 and -19 are located in tight junctions of ameloblasts in the mouse tooth germ where they play a role in regulating extracellular pH, which is critical for processing and secretion of extracellular matrix proteins (<citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fphys.2017.00326" pmid="28596736" pmcid="PMC5442167" count="1">Bardet et al., 2017</citation>; <citation rid="B92" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmedgenet-2016-103956" pmid="27530400" count="1">Yamaguti et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">Cldn3</italic> knockout mice exhibit enamel defects caused by excess accumulation of extracellular matrix proteins in the forming enamel and mutations in <italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic> are associated with Amelogenesis Imperfecta, a genetic disorder characterized by tooth enamel defects (<citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fphys.2017.00326" pmid="28596736" pmcid="PMC5442167" count="1">Bardet et al., 2017</citation>; <citation rid="B92" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmedgenet-2016-103956" pmid="27530400" count="1">Yamaguti et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic> p.A128T and <italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic> p.I22T mutations located in the transmembrane domains of these barrier and pore-forming claudins, respectively, could affect the tight junction barrier leading to a pH imbalance in the extracellular space and lack of secretion of extracellular matrix proteins that are critical for mediating the initial contact between apposed neural folds. <sentence_start/>The hypothesis will be explored in future studies to understand the mechanisms by which these claudins affect the tight junction barrier.

More dramatic open NTDs due to failures in apical constriction and convergent extension were caused by pathogenic variants in the cytoplasmic C-terminal domain, <italic toggle="yes">CLDN8</italic> P216L and <italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic> E209G, respectively. <sentence_start/>The NTDs in the <italic toggle="yes">CLDN8</italic> P216L and <italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic> E209G embryos closely resembled those observed in the embryos that were depleted for Cldn3, 4 and 8. <sentence_start/>Apical constriction and convergent extension are both early steps in neural tube morphogenesis that depend on cell-shape remodeling and cell-cell interactions. <sentence_start/>The claudin C-terminal cytoplasmic domain interacts directly with proteins in the tight junction cytoplasmic plaque, which interacts with the actin-cytoskeleton and is a docking site for several regulatory proteins. <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">CLDN8</italic> p.P216L variant is likely to alter the conformation of the cytoplasmic C-terminal tail, while the <italic toggle="yes">CLDN19</italic> p.E209G variant results in loss of a negatively charged amino acid immediately adjacent to the cytoplasmic C-terminal PDZ-binding domain. <sentence_start/>Both of these variants have the potential to disrupt interactions with the cytoplasmic tail, including PDZ-domain adaptor proteins that connect the tight junction to the actin cytoskeleton. <sentence_start/>In particular, the loss of a negatively charged amino acid is predicted to destabilize interactions with partners that play critical roles in neural tube morphogenesis.

The myelomeningocele patient in our study cohort with the <italic toggle="yes">CLDN8</italic> p.P216L variant was of African ancestry. <sentence_start/>Given that the MAF is >3% in both African Americans in the EVS database and Africans in the gnomAD database, we would predict that this variant alone is not sufficient to cause NTDs in humans. <sentence_start/>However, we cannot rule out that it is a risk factor and could predispose the embryo to develop an NTD in the context of a second genetic hit or an environmental insult.

One limitation to our functional validation assay in the chick embryos is our inability to test whether the remaining 5 pathogenic variants generate hypomorphic alleles that may confer significant risk for NTDs in the context of a second mutation or environmental insult. <sentence_start/>Components of the PCP pathway have a well-established role in regulating convergent extension movements during neural tube closure (<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0925-4773(98)00029-x" pmid="9545534" count="1">Greene et al., 1998</citation>; <citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1006/dbio.2002.0673" pmid="12074560" count="1">Goto and Keller, 2002</citation>; <citation rid="B87" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/dev.00123" pmid="12421719" count="1">Wallingford and Harland, 2002</citation>; <citation rid="B58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-213X-10-87" pmid="20704721" pmcid="PMC2930600" count="1">Paudyal et al., 2010</citation>) and mutations in PCP pathway genes have been recognized as risk factors for human NTDs (<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19319979" doi="10.1002/humu.21026" pmcid="PMC2885434" count="1">Kibar et al., 2009</citation>, <citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1399-0004.2010.01515.x" pmid="20738329" pmcid="PMC3000889" count="1">2011</citation>; <citation rid="B62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.21662" pmid="22095531" pmcid="PMC4772123" count="1">Robinson et al., 2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>We previously showed that claudins act upstream of PCP signaling and convergent extension during neural tube closure (<citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ydbio.2017.05.013" pmid="28545845" pmcid="PMC5523803" count="1">Baumholtz et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>Interestingly, four patients with a rare or novel mutation in a <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> gene also carried a PCP gene variant. <sentence_start/>Only one of these four <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> variants caused NTDs in our overexpression assay (<italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic> p. A128T) in the chick embryo. <sentence_start/>However, it is possible that all four act synergistically with the PCP variants, thereby conferring a high risk for NTDs - a two-hit model for NTDs. <sentence_start/>This digenic model for NTDs has been observed in mice carrying mutations in PCP genes where homozygous mice have a closed neural tube (e.g., <italic toggle="yes">Fzd3<sup>-/-</sup></italic> or <italic toggle="yes">Fzd6<sup>-/-</sup></italic>) (<citation rid="B91" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12351730" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.22-19-08563.2002" pmcid="PMC6757770" count="1">Wang et al., 2002</citation>; <citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.0402802101" pmid="15169958" pmcid="PMC438967" count="1">Guo et al., 2004</citation>), while double homozygous mice (e.g., <italic toggle="yes">Fzd3<sup>-/-</sup>;Fzd6<sup>-/-</sup></italic>) develop NTDs (<citation rid="B89" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/jneurosci.4698-05.2005" pmid="16495441" pmcid="PMC6674805" count="1">Wang Y. et al., 2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, heterozygous mice with spinal NTDs (e.g., Vangl2<sup><italic toggle="yes">Lp/</italic>+</sup>) develop craniorachischisis, a severe NTD that affects the entire embryonic axis, when crossed to heterozygous mice carrying a mutations in a second PCP gene (e.g., <italic toggle="yes">Vangl2<sup><italic toggle="yes">Lp/</italic>+</sup>; Scrib<sup><italic toggle="yes">Crc/</italic>+</sup></italic>, <italic toggle="yes">Vangl2<sup><italic toggle="yes">Lp/</italic>+</sup>; Celsr1<sup><italic toggle="yes">Crsh/</italic>+</sup></italic>, <italic toggle="yes">Vangl2<sup><italic toggle="yes">Lp/</italic>+</sup>; Ptk7<sup><italic toggle="yes">chz/</italic>+</sup></italic>) (<citation rid="B51" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/dmm.016758" pmid="25128525" pmcid="PMC4174526" count="1">Murdoch et al., 2014</citation>). <sentence_start/>It would be interesting to determine if there are genetic interactions between the <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">PCP</italic> variants detected in the same patient. <sentence_start/>In addition, the remaining patients should be screened for mutations in PCP genes.

The mechanisms involved in spinal NTDs are thought to differ from those of cranial NTDs; apical constriction is more important for cranial neural tube closure, while convergent extension plays a more critical role in spinal neural tube closure in chick embryos. <sentence_start/>Fusion of the neural folds to form a closed neural tube occurs at the cranial and spinal levels. <sentence_start/>We have shown that claudins are required for apical constriction and convergent extension and thus, mutations in <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> genes may be implicated in both cranial and spinal NTDs. <sentence_start/>In the future, it would be interesting to sequence genomic DNA from patients with cranial NTDs to compare the pathogenesis of rare and novel <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> variants in the different types of NTDs.
Conclusion

Our study highlights the conserved function of claudins among species in neural tube closure and supports the hypothesis that rare deleterious variants in <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> genes are significant risk factors for human spinal NTDs. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, our study demonstrates the importance of validating pathogenicity in a biological system rather than strictly relying on predictive programs: while <italic toggle="yes">CLDN3</italic> p.P134L, <italic toggle="yes">CLDN9</italic> p.S3L, <italic toggle="yes">CLDN18</italic> p.V88I, and <italic toggle="yes">CLDN24</italic> p.G94R were predicted to be pathogenic by all three prediction program, they did not affect the ability of the Cldn protein to localize to tight junctions or cause NTDs in our overexpression assay. <sentence_start/>In contrast, the <italic toggle="yes">CLDN8</italic> p.P216L variant was predicted to be benign SIFT and MutationTaster, yet overexpression of this variant caused a significant increase in NTDs in our overexpression assay. <sentence_start/>This highlights the limitation of relying on <italic toggle="yes">in silico</italic> prediction programs to predict pathogenicity of non-synonymous variants which exploit limited information such as amino evolutionary conservation and properties, and do not consider known protein functional domains or tissue-specific protein functions. <sentence_start/>To our knowledge, this is the first study to identify deleterious variants in <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> genes in patients with NTDs, which further supports the concept that human NTDs are a group of disorders with high genetic heterogeneity, and both <italic toggle="yes">CLDN</italic> and PCP genomic variants contribute to their occurrence. <sentence_start/>These results enhance our understanding of the pathogenesis of NTDs in humans, highlighting the importance of considering variants in the claudin family as new candidates for NTDs in humans.
